title: How high can the price go?

predict.q: Incumbent AC = MC = **10**. Its profit-maximising price is **16**. A hit-and-run entrant would sell **100** units before the incumbent reacts. It enters if its profit while there is greater than its sunk cost of entry. The sunk cost of entry rises step by step from **0** to **600**. What happens to the highest price the incumbent can charge without attracting entry?

options.fb: The number of firms does not set the price. With sunk costs of 0, any price above 10 lets an entrant take a profit and leave.
The threat of entry only bites if entry pays. An entrant that must write off 300 needs a margin above 3 on its 100 units, so prices up to 13 are safe.
Safe price = 10 + sunk cost ÷ 100: 10, 11, 12 … up to the profit-maximising 16 at a sunk cost of 600.
This reverses the effect. Higher sunk costs protect the incumbent, so its safe price rises.

task: Move the sunk-cost slider from 0 up to 600 and watch the highest safe price.

target.do: Move the sunk-cost slider up to 600, then press Check.

takeaway: The higher the sunk costs, the higher the price the incumbent can safely charge. The market is less contestable.
